events.text: Most people think scammers go after big companies, because that's where the money is.

card.text: You just registered a business. Now you're on a list.

events.text: For brand new businesses in Canada, the opposite is often true.

card.text: You just registered a business. Now you're on a list.

events.text: The day you register a business, your name, your address and your business name start showing up in public records.

card.text: You just registered a business. Now you're on a list.

events.text: And some people read those records for a living.
Within weeks, the letters start.
An invoice for a listing you never ordered.
A renewal notice for a trademark that isn't due for years.
A call from someone who says they're with the tax people.

events.text: Here are the scams that go after new Canadian businesses, how each one works, and the five habits that shut almost all of them down.

Here's what school teaches you.
Registering your business is a legal step.
You pick a structure, you file, you pay a fee, you get a number.
Done.
Here's what school doesn't teach you.
Registering is also publishing.
Business registries, the trademark database and the public records behind web addresses are all searchable, on purpose.
That openness is good.
It's how customers check you're real.
But the Competition Bureau says the companies behind fake renewal notices fill them with your trademark image, your contact details and your registration number, all pulled from public records.
And it says directory scammers often already have your details from public or online listings before they ever call you.
So a new owner gets a letter with their real business name, their real address, and their real registration number on it.
Of course it looks legit.
Every detail on it is true.
Except the part where you owe money.
The centre calls the first one false billing.

events.text: They often arrive many months before anything is due.
